Management of Cleft Lip and Palate

A cleft lip is a birth defect where the upper lip fails to form completely, creating a gap that may extend into the nose. It can occur on one side (unilateral) or both sides (bilateral) and may appear as a small notch or a wide opening.

runs.text: occur on one side (unilateral) or both sides (bilateral) and may appear as a small notch or a wide opening.

blocks.text: A cleft palate occurs when the tissues that form the roof of the mouth (palate) do not fully come together during fetal development. This results in an opening that can affect the hard palate (the bony front portion) and/or the soft palate (the soft back portion) of the mouth. Cleft palates can occur with or without a cleft lip

blocks.text: Systemic Diseases Associated with Dental Conditions
Emphasize oral hygiene and regular dental visits
Cardiovascular Diseases (e.g., Hypertension, Angina, Heart Failure)
Gingival hyperplasia (e.g., calcium channel blockers like nifedipine)
Limit epinephrine in local anaesthesia (especially in hypertension)
Avoid treatment in unstable angina or recent MI (<6 months)
Avoid NSAIDs in patients on anticoagulants
Coordinate with physician (CD4 count, viral load)
Avoid invasive procedures if platelet count <50,000/µL
Gastrointestinal Disorders (e.g., Crohn’s disease, Ulcerative colitis, GERD)
Consider antibiotic prophylaxis (if AV shunt present)
Avoid hepatotoxic drugs (e.g., high-dose paracetamol, some antibiotics)
Autoimmune Diseases (e.g., Sjögren’s syndrome, SLE, Rheumatoid arthritis)
Increased risk of caries and candidiasis
